### Demographic trends and intergenerational relations in Asia and the Pacific

Note by the secretariat

Summary

In the present document, the secretariat provides an overview of demographic trends in Asia and the Pacific and their impact on intergenerational relations. The demographic transition and accompanying age structure changes are affecting all countries in the region. Multiple generations are living and working side by side, which affects the way societies function and evolve. Intergenerational relations are expressed in many different ways, including living arrangements, consumption and production patterns, economic activity, climate change responses, caregiving, lifelong learning and technology use. The present document contains a discussion of these aspects as they relate to the demographic transition and age structure changes. Good practices are presented, challenges are described and recommendations are made as to how to address these challenges in a forward-looking way. The Committee on Social Development may wish to consider the conclusions and recommendations contained in the present document with a view to inviting the secretariat to continue its work on population and development issues, with a focus on intergenerational relations, within its existing mandate. It may also wish to invite members and associate members to promote and work on intergenerational issues, in particular in the light of the World Summit for Social Development in 2025 and the forthcoming fifth review and appraisal of the Madrid International Plan of Action on Ageing, 2002, in Asia and the Pacific.

### I. Introduction

1. People are at the centre of sustainable development, including those of current and future generations. 1, 2 As countries in Asia and the Pacific transition from high to low fertility and mortality levels, their population age structures are changing. Since more people of different age groups are living together for longer periods, intergenerational relations are of crucial importance to ensure that societies are cohesive and inclusive and that no one is left behind.

2. If policymakers and other stakeholders are to deliver prosperity to present and future generations, they must have the benefit of demographic foresight and forward-looking analysis that relate the effects of demographic change to the way societies of all ages function and evolve. The present document is intended to address that need in the context of the Asia-Pacific region.

### II. Demographic trends

3. As of 2024, Asia and the Pacific is home to about 4.8 billion people, or

58 per cent of the world’s population. That number is projected to increase to 5.1 billion by 2050. However, the rate of population growth has been declining, a trend that is projected to continue (see figure I), with some countries already experiencing population decline. Whereas in the mid-1960s, the population in the region grew at a rate that would see it double roughly every 30 years, at the current rate, doubling will take about 140 years.

4. Because the region is highly diverse in terms of geography, economic and social development and demographic trends, the aggregate regional figures mask greater variation at the national and subnational levels. However, the general trend is clear: population growth is declining and population age structures are shifting towards a greater number and share of older persons, while in many countries the number of young people remains high.

A. Demographic transition

5. Over recent decades, countries in the region have undergone the demographic transition – the decline from high to low levels of mortality and fertility (see figure II) – followed by population ageing, smaller family sizes, more people living in urban areas and larger numbers of internal and international migrants. These changes are the result of socioeconomic development and thus a cause for celebration.

Figure II 
Total fertility rate and life expectancy at birth in Asia and the Pacific and 
by subregion, 1950–2050 

Source: ESCAP calculations based on United Nations, Department of Economic and Social Affairs, World Population Prospects 2024 (see figure I).

6. Total fertility declined from 5.6 births per woman in the mid-1960s to 3.2 in 1990 and 1.8 in 2024. This is mainly attributable to increased access to health care (including sexual and reproductive health services), better birth and health outcomes, greater access to quality education and increased participation of women in the labour force. The total fertility rate is projected to remain at about 1.8 births per woman for all of Asia and the Pacific for the near future. The number of countries at or above the replacement level (2.1 births per woman, which is the level required to maintain a population size

over the long term) fell from 57 in the mid-1960s to 50 in 1990 and 28 in 2024. Over the same interval, the number of countries with below-replacement-level fertility rates increased from 1 in the mid-1960s to 8 in 1990 and 30 in 2024. By 2050, it is projected that 40 countries will have fertility rates at or below the replacement level. Moreover, very low fertility, which is defined as a total fertility rate below 1.5 births per woman, and lowest-low fertility, which is a total fertility rate below 1.3 births per woman, can be observed in several countries in Asia and the Pacific (see table 1). By mid-2050, the number of deaths will exceed the number of births in the region for the first time.

7. Over the same period, life expectancy at birth increased from 51.5 years in the mid-1960s to 64.1 in 1990 and 74.7 in 2024. By 2050, life expectancy at birth is projected to increase by another 4.6 years. More people are surviving to old age, and those who do are living longer. For example, in the region, life expectancy at age 60 is projected to increase from 21.0 years in 2024 to 23.6 years in 2050, which represents a rise of 12 per cent. For people aged 80 years or over, life expectancy is projected to increase from 8.1 to 9.4 years over the same period, which represents a rise of 16 per cent. Thus, the older the age group, the more significant are the expected relative gains in life expectancy.

8. In almost all age groups, reductions in mortality have been substantially more pronounced among women than men. For example, the female advantage in life expectancy at birth increased from 3.2 years in the mid-1960s to 5.4 years in 2024 for the region as a whole, although there are variations by country. By 2050, this gender gap is projected to narrow to 4.6 years. Female life expectancy at birth now exceeds 80 years in 16 countries and areas in the region, representing 38 per cent of its total population. This contrasts with eight countries and areas where male life expectancy at birth surpasses 80 years, representing 5 per cent of the total population. By 2050, in more than 29 countries and areas in the region, female longevity is projected to surpass 80 years of age, representing 45 per cent of the total population, while men are projected to live beyond 80 years of age in only 14 countries and areas, representing 32 per cent of the total population. The increase in the number of longer-lived women presents a particular challenge for the Governments of

B24-00298 5 countries in which women are less likely to be covered by social protection, as it increases the risk of poverty in old age.

9. The demographic transition unfolds in stages, with population growth tending to first accelerate and then slow. It is accompanied by changes in the population age structure, eventually leading to an increase in the number and share of older persons. In many countries in Asia and the Pacific, the demographic transition has occurred rapidly, providing little time for societies to adjust.

B. First and second demographic dividends

10. Due to reductions in fertility, the relative size of successive birth cohorts begins to decline. Since the decline in the size of younger age cohorts is not immediately counterbalanced by increases in birth cohorts at older ages, the share of the working-age population temporarily grows relative to the combined shares of younger and older population groups. The growth of the share of the working-age population can be a window of opportunity for accelerated economic growth and social development, and it is often referred to as the “first demographic dividend”. Having more people in the workforce and fewer dependants frees up resources for investment in economic development and family welfare. Other things being equal, per capita income also grows more rapidly. Governments can maximize the benefits of the first demographic dividend by investing in education; health; productive employment opportunities and decent work; and gender equality and the empowerment of women.

11. After the onset of the first demographic dividend, the working-age population remains relatively large for several decades. Eventually, population ageing sets in, defined as the growth in the share of the older population relative to the younger and working-age population. At this stage, a second demographic dividend can occur if a productive workforce prepares for longer life through increased savings and investment, leading to a further rise in productivity and national incomes. This period can be sustained as long as savings are generated and invested in human, physical and environmental capital. 3

12. Research shows that the onset, duration and end of demographic dividends vary considerably across the region. In many countries, the window of opportunity for harnessing the benefits of the first demographic dividend has already closed (e.g. Australia, China, Japan, the Republic of Korea, Singapore, Thailand and Viet Nam).
